html:
An empire that ruled most of the Indian subcontinent at its height, founded in 1526 by Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan. Its real power collapsed after 1707, but the emperors lived on as figureheads until the British deposed the last one in 1857.

Babur came from Central Asia and defeated the last Delhi sultan at the First Battle of Panipat with the help of cannon and matchlocks. His son Humayun lost the throne to Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and won it back in 1555.

The great emperors:

  • Akbar (1556 to 1605) built the empire's system of ranked officials and land revenue, made alliances with Rajput kings, and welcomed debate between faiths.
  • Jahangir (1605 to 1627) presided over a golden age of painting.
  • Shah Jahan (1628 to 1658) built the Taj Mahal and a new capital at Delhi.
  • Aurangzeb (1658 to 1707) pushed the empire to its largest size but spent his last decades in costly wars in the Deccan, above all against the Marathas.

The empire was among the richest states in the world. Its cotton cloth was sold across Asia, Africa and Europe; Indian calicoes became a European craze. Its architecture, painting, music and the Urdu language blended Persian and Indian traditions.

After Aurangzeb, governors in Bengal, Hyderabad and Awadh became independent, the Marathas spread north, and in 1739 the Persian ruler Nadir Shah sacked Delhi. After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 the East India Company took over Bengal, and the emperor became its pensioner. The last emperor, Bahadur Shah II, was named leader of the 1857 rebellion; the British exiled him to Rangoon and ended the dynasty.
